## Matrix Algebra for Regression

$$y_i= \beta_0 + \beta_1x_{i1} + \beta_2x_{i2} + \dots + \beta_kx_{ik} + \epsilon_i, \quad \epsilon_i \stackrel{iid}{\sim} N(0, \sigma^2), \quad i = 1, 2, \dots, n$$

<!-- - $\epsilon_i \stackrel{iid}{\sim} N(0, \sigma^2)$ -->

. . .


$$\bf y = \bf X \bbeta + \beps$$ where

$$\begin{align}
\bf y = \begin{bmatrix}
y_1 \\
y_2 \\
\vdots \\
y_n \end{bmatrix},\quad
\bf X = \begin{bmatrix}
  1 & x_{11} & x_{12} & \cdots & x_{1k} \\
  1 & x_{21} & x_{22} & \cdots & x_{2k} \\
  \vdots & \vdots  & \vdots  & \ddots & \vdots  \\
  1 & x_{n1} & x_{n2} & \cdots & x_{nk} \end{bmatrix}, \quad
\bbeta = \begin{bmatrix}
\beta_0 \\
\beta_1 \\
\vdots \\
\beta_k \end{bmatrix} , \quad
\beps = \begin{bmatrix}
\epsilon_1 \\
\epsilon_2 \\
\vdots \\
\epsilon_n\end{bmatrix}
\end{align}$$

::: alert
The main goal is not matrix computation by hand. It is to understand the geometry and algebra behind

$$
{\bf b}=({\bf X}'{\bf X})^{-1}{\bf X}'{\bf y}.
$$
:::


## Matrix
- A **matrix** ${\bf A}$ that has $n$ rows and $m$ columns is defined as $${\bf A} = (a_{ij})_{n \times m}\begin{bmatrix} a_{11} & a_{12} & \cdots & a_{1m} \\ a_{21} & a_{22} & \cdots & a_{2m} \\ \vdots  & \vdots  & \ddots & \vdots  \\ a_{n1} & a_{n2} & \cdots & a_{nm} \end{bmatrix}_{n \times m}$$

. . .

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| echo: true
(A <- matrix(data = 1:6, 
             nrow = 2, ncol = 3))
class(A)
```
:::



::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| echo: true
attributes(A)
```
:::
::::

. . .

::: question
But what is the geometrical meaning of matrices?
:::


::: notes
- First index is for row and the second index is for column
- Use command matrix() to create a matrix.
- A matrix is a two-dimensional analog of a vector.
- Like **all** elements of a matrix must be of the **same type.**
:::



## Matrices as Linear Transformations

{{< video https://youtu.be/kYB8IZa5AuE width="100%" height="80%" >}}

::: {.footer}
3Blue1Brown, *Essence of Linear Algebra*, Chapter 3
:::


::: notes
- A matrix is actually a numerical representation of a linear transformation in a linear space which is a function that takes an vector as an input and produces another vector as an output.
- If we use the grid lines to represent the entire coordinate system, we will see that when we use (1, 0) and (0, 1) as the two bases, all lines are vertical and horizontal, showing, for example, the integer values of each coordinate. 
- Linear transformation means we stretch or rotate the lines, but at the same time, all lines remains lines and origin remain fixed.
- Grids lines are parallel and evenly spaced after linear transformation.
- (-1, 3) is the transformed vector of (-1, 2) when the two new transformed basis are (3, 1) and (1, 2)
:::


## Column Vector
- If $m = 1$, it becomes a $n$ by 1 matrix or a **column vector** of size $n$.
$$\small {\bf y} = \begin{bmatrix} y_{1}  \\ y_{2}  \\ \vdots  \\  y_{n} \end{bmatrix}_{n \times 1} \quad {\bf 1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1  \\ 1  \\ \vdots  \\  1 \end{bmatrix}_{n \times 1}$$

. . .

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
A

## 2nd column
A[, 2]

## becomes a numeric vector
class(A[, 2]) 
```
:::



::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
## keep its matrix class
A[, 2, drop = FALSE] 
class(A[, 2, drop = FALSE])  
```
:::
::::




## Row Vector
- If $n = 1$, it becomes a $1$ by $m$ matrix or a **row vector** of size $m$.
$${\bf x} = \begin{bmatrix} x_{1} &  x_{2}  & \dots  &  x_{m} \end{bmatrix}_{1 \times m}$$
- By default, a vector means a *column* vector.

```{r}
## 2nd row
A[2, , drop = FALSE]
## keep its matrix class
class(A[2, , drop = FALSE]) 
```


## Vectors: Addition and Scalar Multiplication

Let

$$
{\bf u}=
\begin{bmatrix}
u_1\\u_2
\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
{\bf v}=
\begin{bmatrix}
v_1\\v_2
\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Then

$$
{\bf u}+{\bf v}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
u_1+v_1\\
u_2+v_2
\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
c{\bf u}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
cu_1\\
cu_2
\end{bmatrix}.
$$

```{r}
u <- c(1, 2)
v <- c(3, -1)

u + v
2 * u
```


## Linear Combinations

A **linear combination** of vectors ${\bf v}_1,\dots,{\bf v}_k$ is

$$
c_1{\bf v}_1+\cdots+c_k{\bf v}_k.
$$

For example,

$$
2
\begin{bmatrix}1\\0\end{bmatrix}
+
3
\begin{bmatrix}0\\1\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}2\\3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

. . .

::: alert
Matrix multiplication ${\bf Xb}$ is a linear combination of the **columns of ${\bf X}$**.
:::

If

$$
{\bf X}=
\begin{bmatrix}
{\bf x}_1 & {\bf x}_2 & \cdots & {\bf x}_p
\end{bmatrix},
$$

then

$$
{\bf Xb}
=
b_1{\bf x}_1+\cdots+b_p{\bf x}_p.
$$


## Span and Column Space

The **span** of vectors ${\bf v}_1,\ldots,{\bf v}_k$ is the set of all their linear combinations:

$$
\operatorname{span}({\bf v}_1,\dots,{\bf v}_k)
=
\left\{
c_1{\bf v}_1+\cdots+c_k{\bf v}_k
\right\}.
$$

For a matrix

$$
{\bf X}=
\begin{bmatrix}
{\bf x}_1 & \cdots & {\bf x}_p
\end{bmatrix},
$$

the **column space** is

$$
\operatorname{Col}({\bf X})
=
\operatorname{span}({\bf x}_1,\dots,{\bf x}_p).
$$

::: alert
In regression, every fitted-value vector

$$
\hat{\bf y}={\bf Xb}
$$

must lie in $\operatorname{Col}({\bf X})$.
:::


## Why Column Space Matters for Regression

Suppose

$$
{\bf X}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
{\bf 1} & {\bf x}_1 & {\bf x}_2
\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Then every possible fitted vector has the form

$$
{\bf Xb}
=
b_0{\bf 1}+b_1{\bf x}_1+b_2{\bf x}_2.
$$

. . .

- Changing ${\bf b}$ moves us to a different point in $\operatorname{Col}({\bf X})$.
- Least squares chooses the point in $\operatorname{Col}({\bf X})$ closest to ${\bf y}$.
- This geometric viewpoint will explain the normal equations later.

## Transpose
- Let ${\bf A}$ be an $n \times m$ matrix. The transpose of ${\bf A}$, denoted by ${\bf A}'$ or ${\bf A}^T$, is a $m \times n$ matrix whose columns are the rows of ${\bf A}$.
$${\bf A} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 4 & 5 & 6 \\ \end{bmatrix} \quad {\bf A}' =\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 4 \\ 2 & 5 \\ 3 & 6\end{bmatrix}$$
$${\bf X}_{n \times 2}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & x_1 \\ 1 & x_{2} \\ \vdots  & \vdots  \\ 1 & x_n \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} {\bf 1} & {\bf x} \end{bmatrix}$$
$${\bf X}'_{2 \times n} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & \cdots & 1 \\ x_1 & x_2 & \cdots & x_n \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} {\bf 1}' \\ {\bf x}' \end{bmatrix}$$


## Transpose in R
```{r}
A
t(A)
```


## Determinant

For a square matrix ${\bf A}=\begin{bmatrix}a & b\\ c & d\end{bmatrix},$

the determinant is $\det({\bf A})=ad-bc.$

```{r}
A2 <- matrix(c(2, 1,
               3, 4), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
A2
det(A2)
```

. . .

For a square matrix,

$$
\boxed{\det({\bf A})\ne0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
{\bf A}\text{ is invertible}}
$$

::: notes
- Geometrically, the absolute determinant gives the factor by which the linear transformation scales area in 2D or volume in higher dimensions.
- A zero determinant means that the transformation collapses the space into a lower-dimensional subspace.
:::


## Determinant: Geometric Interpretation

For a $2\times2$ matrix, $|\det({\bf A})|$ is the factor by which areas are scaled.

- $|\det({\bf A})|>1$: area expands.
- $0<|\det({\bf A})|<1$: area contracts.
- $\det({\bf A})<0$: orientation is reversed.
- $\det({\bf A})=0$: the plane is collapsed to a line or a point.

::: alert
If $\det({\bf A})=0$, some column information is redundant.  
That is exactly the kind of issue that appears with perfect multicollinearity.
:::


## Linear Independence
<!-- - Vectors ${\bf v}_1, {\bf v}_2, \dots, {\bf v}_k$ is said to be **linearly dependent** if there exists scalars $c_{1},c_{2},\dots,c_{k},$ not all zero, such that  -->
<!-- $$c_{1}{\bf v}_1 + c_{2}{\bf v}_2 + \cdots + c_{k}{\bf v}_k = \bf 0$$ -->
- Vectors ${\bf v}_1, {\bf v}_2, \dots, {\bf v}_k$ is said to be **linearly independent** if for scalars $c_{1},c_{2},\dots,c_{k} \in \mathbf{R},$
$$c_{1}{\bf v}_1 + c_{2}{\bf v}_2 + \cdots + c_{k}{\bf v}_k = \bf 0$$ can only be satisfied by $c_i = 0$ for all $i = 1, 2, \dots, k$.

::: question
Are ${\bf v}_1 = (1, 1)'$ and ${\bf v}_2 = (-3, 2)'$ linearly independent?
:::

. . .

Ways to check linear independence:

- solve the homogeneous linear system
$\begin{bmatrix} 1 & -3 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} c_1 \\ c_2 \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}$ for $c_1$ and $c_2$.

- check if $\text{det} \left( \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -3 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \right)$ is non-zero.



## Linear Independence

```{r}
V <- matrix(c(1, 1, -3, 2), nrow = 2, ncol = 2)
solve(a = V, b = rep(0, 2))
det(V)
```


::: notes
- A is invertible, that is, A has an inverse, is nonsingular, and is nondegenerate.
- A is row-equivalent to the n-by-n identity matrix In.
- A is column-equivalent to the n-by-n identity matrix In.
- A has n pivot positions.
- A has full rank; that is, rank A = n.
- Based on the rank A=n, the equation Ax = 0 has only the trivial solution x = 0. and the equation Ax = b has exactly one solution for each b in Kn.
- The kernel (null space) of A is trivial
- The columns of A are linearly independent.
- The columns of A span Kn.
- The columns of A form a basis of Kn.
- det A ≠ 0.
- The number 0 is not an eigenvalue of A.
- The transpose AT is an invertible matrix 
:::



##  Rank
- The **rank** of a matrix ${\bf A} = \begin{bmatrix} {\bf a}_1 & {\bf a}_2 & \cdots & {\bf a}_m \end{bmatrix}$ is the *number of linearly independent columns* (dimension of the column space).

- If $k$ of the $m$ column vectors ${\bf a}_1, {\bf a}_2, \dots, {\bf a}_m$ are linearly independent, the rank of ${\bf A}$ is $k$. 

- The remaining $m-k$ columns of ${\bf A}$ can be written as a linear combination of the $k$ linearly independent columns.


::: notes
- If $k = m$, it is full rank
- If $k$ of the $n$ column vectors ${\bf a}_1, {\bf a}_2, \dots, {\bf a}_n$ are linearly independent, the rank of ${\bf A}$ is $k$. The remaining $n-k$ columns can be written as a linear combination of the $k$ columns.
- The vectors ${\bf v}_1, {\bf v}_2, \dots, {\bf v}_k$ is said to be **linearly dependent** if there exist scalars $c_{1},c_{2},\dots,c_{k},$ not all zero, such that 
$$c_{1}{\bf v}_1 + c_{2}{\bf v}_2 + \cdots + c_{k}{\bf v}_k = \bf 0$$
- The column vectors ${\bf v}_1, {\bf v}_2, \dots, {\bf v}_k$ is said to be **linearly independent** if it is not linearly dependent, that is, if
$$c_{1}{\bf v}_1 + c_{2}{\bf v}_2 + \cdots + c_{k}{\bf v}_k = \bf 0$$ can only be satisfied by $c_i = 0, i = 1, 2, \dots, k.$
:::



## Rank
```{r}
(M <- matrix(1:9, nrow = 3, ncol = 3))
# install.packages("Matrix")
library(Matrix)
rankMatrix(M)[1]
```

::: question
Can you see why the rank is 2, meaning that one column can be written as a linear combo of the other two?
:::

. . .

- ${\bf a}_3 = 2{\bf a_2}-{\bf a}_1$

```{r}
2 * M[, 2] - 1 * M[, 1]
```

::: notes
- Find the row or column basis of A using reduced row echelon form
- the dimension of the vector space generated (or spanned) by its columns
- dimension: number of basis in the vector space.
:::



## Linear Systems: ${\bf Ax}={\bf b}$

A system of linear equations can be written compactly as

$$
{\bf Ax}={\bf b}.
$$

Example:

$$
\begin{aligned}
2x_1+x_2 &=5,\\
x_1+3x_2 &=7.
\end{aligned}
$$

becomes

$$
\begin{bmatrix}
2&1\\
1&3
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}
x_1\\x_2
\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
5\\7
\end{bmatrix}.
$$

```{r}
A_sys <- matrix(c(2, 1,
                  1, 3), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
b_sys <- c(5, 7)

solve(A_sys, b_sys)
```


## Unique Solutions and Rank

For a square matrix ${\bf A}_{n\times n}$, the following statements are equivalent:

- ${\bf A}$ has full rank $n$.
- The columns of ${\bf A}$ are linearly independent.
- $\det({\bf A})\ne0$.
- ${\bf A}^{-1}$ exists.
- ${\bf Ax}={\bf b}$ has a unique solution for every ${\bf b}$.

. . .

::: alert
Regression connection:

$$
{\bf b}=({\bf X}'{\bf X})^{-1}{\bf X}'{\bf y}
$$

requires ${\bf X}$ to have full column rank.
:::


## Operations: Addition

- **Addition:** ${\bf A + B}$ is adding the corresponding elements together $a_{ij} + b_{ij}$. 

- ${\bf A}$ and ${\bf B}$ must have an *equal* number of rows and columns.

::: {.column width="50%"}

```{r}
A

A + B
```

:::

```{r}
A + B
```

:::

## Operations: Multiplication
- **Multiplication:** The product of matrices ${\bf A}$ and ${\bf B}$ is denoted as ${\bf AB}$.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| out-width: 55%
knitr::include_graphics("https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/1/18/Matrix_multiplication_qtl1.svg")
```

- The number of columns in ${\bf A}$ must be equal to the number of rows ${\bf B}$. 
- The result matrix ${\bf C}$ has the number of rows of ${\bf A}$ and the number of columns of the ${\bf B}$.


::: notes
- The number of columns in the first matrix ${\bf A}$ must be equal to the number of rows in the second matrix of ${\bf B}$. 
- The resulting matrix ${\bf C}$ has dimension of the number of rows of the first and the number of columns of the second matrix.
:::


## Operations: Multiplication

- ${\bf A}{\bf B} \ne {\bf B}{\bf A}$ in general.

- $({\bf A}{\bf B})' =  {\bf B}'{\bf A}'$. 

<br>

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}

```{r}
(C <- matrix(1:6, 3, 2))
(D <- matrix(2:7, 2, 3))
C %*% D
```

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

::: fragment
```{r}
#| error: true
D %*% C
t(C %*% D)
t(D) %*% t(C)
```
:::

:::

## [R Lab]{.pink} Crossproducts

In regression we repeatedly encounter products such as ${\bf X}'{\bf X}$ and ${\bf X}'{\bf y}.$ In R,

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}

::: shrink-code
```{r}
X_cp <- matrix(1:6, nrow = 3, ncol = 2)
y_cp <- c(2, 4, 7)

t(X_cp) %*% X_cp
crossprod(X_cp)

t(X_cp) %*% y_cp
crossprod(X_cp, y_cp)
```
:::

`crossprod(X, Y)` computes ${\bf X}'{\bf Y}$ directly.

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

::: fragment
Similarly,

```{r}
tcrossprod(X_cp)
```

computes ${\bf X}{\bf X}'$.
:::

<br>

::: fragment
::: alert
`crossprod()` and `tcrossprod()` are convenient and efficient for matrix products that occur constantly in regression.
:::
:::

:::
::::

# Geometry of Vectors

## Inner Product (Dot Product)

For vectors ${\bf x},{\bf y}\in\mathbb R^n$,

$$
{\bf x}'{\bf y}
=
\sum_{i=1}^n x_i y_i.
$$

```{r}
x <- c(1, 2, 3)
y <- c(4, -1, 2)

sum(x * y)
t(x) %*% y
```

The dot product measures how strongly two vectors point in the same direction.



## Outer Product

For column vectors ${\bf x}\in\mathbb R^m$ and ${\bf y}\in\mathbb R^n$,

$$
{\bf x}{\bf y}'
$$

is an $m\times n$ matrix.

For example,

$$
\begin{bmatrix}1\\2\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}3&4&5\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
3&4&5\\
6&8&10
\end{bmatrix}.
$$

```{r}
x <- c(1, 2)
y <- c(3, 4, 5)

x %o% y
```

::: notes
- Contrast the inner product x'y, which is a scalar, with the outer product xy', which is a matrix.
- Outer products appear naturally in covariance matrices and matrix decompositions.
:::


## Length and Distance

The Euclidean norm of ${\bf x}$ is $\|{\bf x}\|=\sqrt{{\bf x}'{\bf x}}=\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2}.$

The distance between ${\bf x}$ and ${\bf y}$ is $\|{\bf x}-{\bf y}\|.$

```{r}
x <- c(1, 2)
y <- c(4, 6)

sqrt(sum(x^2))
sqrt(sum((x - y)^2))
```

::: alert
Least squares minimizes a squared Euclidean distance:

$$
\|{\bf y}-{\bf Xb}\|^2.
$$
:::


## Angle Between Vectors

The angle $\theta$ between nonzero vectors ${\bf x}$ and ${\bf y}$ satisfies

$$
\cos(\theta)
=
\frac{{\bf x}'{\bf y}}
{\|{\bf x}\|\,\|{\bf y}\|}.
$$

```{r}
x <- c(1, 0)
y <- c(1, 1)

theta <- acos(
  sum(x * y) /
    (sqrt(sum(x^2)) * sqrt(sum(y^2)))
)

theta * 180 / pi
```

- $\theta=0^\circ$: same direction
- $\theta=90^\circ$: orthogonal
- $\theta=180^\circ$: opposite directions


## Orthogonality

Two vectors are **orthogonal** if

$$
{\bf x}'{\bf y}=0.
$$

```{r}
x <- c(1, 2)
y <- c(2, -1)

t(x) %*% y
```

::: alert
In least squares,

$$
{\bf X}'{\bf e}={\bf 0}.
$$

The residual vector is orthogonal to every column of ${\bf X}$.
:::


## Projection onto a Vector

The projection of ${\bf y}$ onto a nonzero vector ${\bf x}$ is

$$
\operatorname{proj}_{\bf x}({\bf y})
=
\frac{{\bf x}'{\bf y}}{{\bf x}'{\bf x}}{\bf x}.
$$

```{r}
x <- c(1, 2)
y <- c(4, 1)

proj_y <- as.numeric(t(x) %*% y / as.numeric(t(x) %*% x)) * x
proj_y

# residual from projection
e <- y - proj_y
t(x) %*% e
```

::: notes
- The residual from the projection is orthogonal to x.
- This is the one-dimensional version of least squares projection onto the column space of X.
:::


## Special Matrices: Symmetric and Identity
- A square matrix $(m = n)$ ${\bf A}_{n \times n}$ is a **symmetric** matrix if ${\bf A = A}'$.

$${\bf A} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2  \\ 2 & 5 \\ \end{bmatrix} \quad {\bf A}' =\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 5 \end{bmatrix}$$


- A square matrix ${\bf I}_{n \times n}$ whose diagonal elements are 1's and off diagonal elements are 0's is called an **identity** matrix of order $n$.
$${\bf I} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & \cdots & 0 \\ \vdots  & \vdots  & \ddots & \vdots  \\ 0 & 0 & \cdots & 1 \end{bmatrix}$$


::: notes
- If the inverse exists, it is unique.
:::



## Identity and Diagonal Matrix

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
## Identity matrix
I <- diag(5)
I
## A diagonal matrix
diag(c(4, 2, 5))
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

```{r}
## Extract diagonal elements
D <- matrix(1:4, 2, 2)
D
diag(D)
```
:::
::::



## Inverse Matrix
- The **inverse** of a square matrix ${\bf A}$, denoted by ${\bf A}^{-1}$, is a square matrix such that $${\bf A}^{-1}{\bf A} = {\bf A}{\bf A}^{-1} = {\bf I}$$

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
D
D_inv <- solve(D)
D_inv
```
:::


::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
D_inv %*% D
D %*% D_inv
```
:::
::::




## Inverse vs. Solving a System in R

Mathematically, ${\bf x}={\bf A}^{-1}{\bf b}$ solves ${\bf Ax}={\bf b}.$

In computation, it is usually better to solve the system directly:

```{r}
A <- matrix(c(4, 1,
              1, 3), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
b <- c(1, 2)

# preferred
solve(A, b)

# mathematically equivalent
solve(A) %*% b
```

::: alert
Use `solve(A, b)` when you want the solution to ${\bf Ax}={\bf b}$.

Avoid forming an inverse explicitly unless you actually need the inverse matrix.
:::


## Idempotent, Orthogonal, Positive Definite
- A square matrix ${\bf A}$ is **idempotent** if ${\bf A}{\bf A} = {\bf A}$.
- A square matrix ${\bf A}$ is **orthogonal** if ${\bf A}^{-1} = {\bf A}'$ and hence ${\bf A}'{\bf A} = {\bf I}$.

. . .

- Let ${\bf A}$ be a $n \times n$ matrix and ${\bf y}$ be a $n \times 1$ vector. $${\bf y}'{\bf A} {\bf y} = \sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^na_{ij}y_iy_j$$ is called a **quadratic form** of ${\bf y}$.

. . .

- A symmetric matrix ${\bf A}$ is said to be 
  <!-- + ${\bf A}' = {\bf A}$ -->
  + **positive definite** if ${\bf y}'{\bf A} {\bf y} > 0$ for all ${\bf y \ne 0}$.
  + **positive semi-definite** if ${\bf y}'{\bf A} {\bf y} \ge 0$ for all ${\bf y \ne 0}$ and ${\bf y}'{\bf A} {\bf y} = 0$ for some ${\bf y \ne 0}$.
- If ${\bf A}$ is symmetric and idempotent, then ${\bf A}$ is positive semi-definite.

::: notes
- How about negative definite
:::



## Positive Definite Matrices and Regression

If ${\bf X}$ has full column rank, then for every nonzero vector ${\bf a}$,

$$
{\bf a}'{\bf X}'{\bf X}{\bf a}
=
({\bf Xa})'({\bf Xa})
=
\|{\bf Xa}\|^2
>0.
$$

Therefore, $\boxed{{\bf X}'{\bf X}\text{ is positive definite}}$ and hence invertible.

. . .

If the columns of ${\bf X}$ are linearly dependent, there is a nonzero ${\bf a}$ with ${\bf Xa}={\bf 0},$

so

$$
{\bf a}'{\bf X}'{\bf X}{\bf a}=0,
$$

and ${\bf X}'{\bf X}$ is not positive definite.

::: alert
This is another way to understand why perfect multicollinearity prevents unique least-squares coefficients.
:::


## Special Matrices: Idempotent, Orthogonal
:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
## Idempotent and symmetric matrix
(A <- matrix(1, 2, 2)/2)
A %*% A
## positive semi-definite
y <- c(-2, 5); t(y) %*% A %*% y
z <- c(-1, 1); t(z) %*% A %*% z
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: fragment
```{r}
## Orthogonal matrix
(E <- matrix(c(0, 1, 0, -1, 0, 0, 0, 0, -1), 
             nrow = 3, ncol = 3))
solve(E)
t(E) %*% E
```
:::
:::
::::



## Trace
- The **trace** of ${\bf A}_{n \times n}$, denoted by $\text{tr}({\bf A})$, is defined as $$\text{tr}({\bf A}) = a_{11} + a_{22} + \dots + a_{nn}$$

- $\text{tr}({\bf A}{\bf B}) = \text{tr}({\bf B}{\bf A})$


```{r}
(G <- matrix(1:6, 3, 2)); (H <- matrix(6:1, 2, 3));
sum(diag(G%*%H)); sum(diag(H%*%G))
```




## Useful Properties of the Trace

For conformable matrices,

$$
\operatorname{tr}({\bf A}+{\bf B})
=
\operatorname{tr}({\bf A})
+
\operatorname{tr}({\bf B}),
$$

$$
\operatorname{tr}(c{\bf A})
=
c\,\operatorname{tr}({\bf A}),
$$

and

$$
\boxed{
\operatorname{tr}({\bf AB})
=
\operatorname{tr}({\bf BA})
}.
$$

For a symmetric matrix,

$$
\operatorname{tr}({\bf A})=\sum_j \lambda_j,\quad \textrm{and}\quad \operatorname{det}({\bf A})=\prod_j \lambda_j.
$$

where $\lambda_j$'s are eigenvalues of ${\bf A}.$


## Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors

- For a square matrix ${\bf A}$, if we can find a scalar $\lambda$ and a non-zero vector ${\bf x}$ such that $${\bf Ax} = \lambda {\bf x},$$
  + $\lambda$ is an **eigenvalue** of ${\bf A}$
  + ${\bf x}$ is a corresponding **eigenvector** of ${\bf A}$.

- A general $n\times n$ matrix has $n$ eigenvalues over the complex numbers when counted with multiplicity, but it may not have $n$ linearly independent eigenvectors.
- A **real symmetric** matrix has $n$ real eigenvalues and an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors.




## Geometric Meaning of Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors

{{< video https://youtu.be/PFDu9oVAE-g width="100%" height="80%" >}}

::: {.footer}
3Blue1Brown, *Essence of Linear Algebra*, Chapter 14
:::

## Eigen-decomposition
- **Eigen-decomposition**: Any symmetric matrix ${\bf A}_{n \times n}$ can be decomposed as $${\bf A} = {\bf V\bsLambda V'}$$

- $\bsLambda$ is a $n \times n$ diagnonal matrix whose elements are eigenvalues $\lambda_j$ of ${\bf A}$
  $$\bsLambda = \begin{bmatrix} \lambda_1 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\ 0 & \lambda_2 & \cdots & 0 \\ \vdots  & \vdots  & \ddots & \vdots  \\ 0 & 0 & \cdots & \lambda_n \end{bmatrix}$$
  
- ${\bf V} = [{\bf v}_1 \quad {\bf v}_2 \quad \dots \quad {\bf v}_n]$ is a $n \times n$ orthogonal matrix whose columns are the eigenvectors of ${\bf A}.$



## Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors

Let ${\bf A} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$ be a square matrix with eigenvalues
$\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_n$.

- $\operatorname{tr}({\bf A}) = \sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i$
- $\det({\bf A}) = \prod_{i=1}^n \lambda_i$
- If ${\bf A}$ is symmetric, $\operatorname{rank}({\bf A}) = \#\{i : \lambda_i \neq 0\}$
- If ${\bf A}$ is symmetric, all $\lambda_i \in \mathbb{R}$



## Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors
:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
(A <- matrix(c(5, 1, 1, 2), 2, 2))
eigen_decomp <- eigen(A)
(lam <- eigen_decomp$values)
(V <- eigen_decomp$vectors)
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
V %*% diag(lam) %*% t(V)
sum(diag(A))
sum(lam)
det(A)
prod(lam)
```
:::
::::

## Eigenvalues and Positive Definiteness

For a real symmetric matrix ${\bf A}$:

- ${\bf A}$ is positive definite iff all eigenvalues are positive.
- ${\bf A}$ is positive semi-definite iff all eigenvalues are nonnegative.
- ${\bf A}$ is singular iff at least one eigenvalue is zero.

::: alert
For regression, small eigenvalues of ${\bf X}'{\bf X}$ indicate nearly dependent predictor directions and therefore potential multicollinearity.
:::


## Eigenvalues of ${\bf X}'{\bf X}$

```{r}
set.seed(123)

x1 <- rnorm(100)
x2 <- x1 + rnorm(100, sd = 0.05)

X_col <- cbind(1, x1, x2)

eigen(t(X_col) %*% X_col)$values
```

Compare with less-correlated predictors:

```{r}
x3 <- rnorm(100)
X_ok <- cbind(1, x1, x3)

eigen(t(X_ok) %*% X_ok)$values
```

::: notes
- When two columns are almost linearly dependent, one direction in X'X has very little variation.
- That appears as a small eigenvalue.
- We will revisit this idea when we discuss multicollinearity.
:::



# Matrix Decompositions

## Why Matrix Decompositions?

A matrix decomposition writes a matrix as a product of simpler matrices.

They are useful for

- solving systems of equations,
- obtaining numerically stable computations,
- understanding the structure and rank of a matrix,
- obtaining low-rank approximations.

We will briefly connect four decompositions to regression:

1. eigenvalue decomposition,
2. Cholesky decomposition,
3. QR decomposition,
4. singular value decomposition.

::: notes
- The goal is not to derive every algorithm.
- Students should recognize what each decomposition does and why regression software uses such decompositions.
:::


## Cholesky Decomposition

For a symmetric positive-definite matrix ${\bf A}$,

$$
\boxed{
{\bf A}={\bf L}{\bf L}'
}
$$

where ${\bf L}$ is lower triangular.

Because ${\bf X}'{\bf X}$ is positive definite when ${\bf X}$ has full column rank, Cholesky decomposition can be used to solve systems involving ${\bf X}'{\bf X}$.

```{r}
A_chol <- matrix(c(4, 2,
                   2, 3), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)

R <- chol(A_chol)
R
t(R) %*% R
```

::: notes
- R returns the upper-triangular factor R such that A = R'R.
- Cholesky is useful for positive-definite systems, including covariance matrices.
:::


## QR Decomposition

For a tall matrix ${\bf X}$ with $n\ge p$, $\boxed{{\bf X}={\bf Q}{\bf R}}$, where

- ${\bf Q}'{\bf Q}={\bf I}$, so the columns of ${\bf Q}$ are orthonormal;
- ${\bf R}$ is upper triangular.

```{r}
X_qr <- matrix(c(1, 1,
                 1, 2,
                 1, 3,
                 1, 4), nrow = 4, byrow = TRUE)
qrX <- qr(X_qr); Q <- qr.Q(qrX); R <- qr.R(qrX)
Q %*% R
```

::: alert
QR decomposition is especially important for least squares because it lets us solve the regression problem **without explicitly forming** $({\bf X}'{\bf X})^{-1}$.
:::


## Least Squares Using QR

Suppose ${\bf X}={\bf Q}{\bf R}.$ Then the least-squares problem $$\min_{\bf b}\|{\bf y}-{\bf Xb}\|^2$$

becomes $$\min_{\bf b}\|{\bf y}-{\bf QRb}\|^2.$$

Using the orthogonality of ${\bf Q}$ leads to the triangular system $\boxed{{\bf Rb}={\bf Q}'{\bf y}}.$

```{r}
y_qr <- c(2, 3, 5, 8)
(b_qr <- backsolve(R, t(Q) %*% y_qr))
coef(lm(y_qr ~ X_qr[, 2]))
```

::: notes
- This is computationally preferable to explicitly computing (X'X)^(-1).
- The details of the numerical algorithm are not needed here; the conceptual point is that orthogonalization simplifies least squares.
:::


# Singular Value Decomposition

## Singular Value Decomposition (SVD)

Every $n\times p$ matrix ${\bf X}$ can be written as

$$
\boxed{
{\bf X}={\bf U}{\bf D}{\bf V}'
}
$$

where

- ${\bf U}$ has orthonormal columns,
- ${\bf V}$ has orthonormal columns,
- ${\bf D}$ is diagonal with nonnegative singular values

$$
d_1\ge d_2\ge\cdots\ge0.
$$

Unlike eigendecomposition, the SVD applies to **rectangular matrices**.


## SVD in R

```{r}
X_demo <- matrix(c(1, 2,
                   2, 1,
                   3, 4), nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE)
sv <- svd(X_demo)
sv$d; sv$u; sv$v
```

Reconstruct ${\bf X}$:

```{r}
sv$u %*% diag(sv$d) %*% t(sv$v)
```


## Rank and Singular Values

The rank of a matrix equals the number of nonzero singular values:

$$
\operatorname{rank}({\bf X})
=
\#\{j:d_j>0\}.
$$

If a singular value is very small rather than exactly zero, the matrix is **nearly rank deficient**.

::: alert
Regression connection:

- zero singular value $\rightarrow$ perfect multicollinearity;
- very small singular value $\rightarrow$ near multicollinearity and unstable coefficient estimates.
:::


## Connecting SVD and ${\bf X}'{\bf X}$

If ${\bf X}={\bf U}{\bf D}{\bf V}'$, then $${\bf X}'{\bf X}={\bf V}{\bf D}^2{\bf V}'.$$

Therefore, $$\lambda_j({\bf X}'{\bf X})=d_j^2.$$

::: alert
The eigenvalues of ${\bf X}'{\bf X}$ are the squared singular values of ${\bf X}$.
:::

This connects

- rank,
- multicollinearity,
- eigendecomposition,
- SVD,
- and least squares.


# Regression Takeaways

## Why Did We Review All This?

| Linear algebra idea | Regression role |
|---|---|
| Linear combination | ${\bf Xb}$ combines columns of ${\bf X}$ |
| Column space | contains all possible fitted-value vectors |
| Rank | determines whether coefficients are uniquely estimable |
| Inner product | defines orthogonality |
| Projection | $\hat{\bf y}$ is projection of ${\bf y}$ onto $\operatorname{Col}({\bf X})$ |
| Inverse / solve | solves the normal equations |
| Positive definiteness | guarantees invertibility of ${\bf X}'{\bf X}$ |
| Eigenvalues / SVD | diagnose dependent or nearly dependent directions |

::: alert
The central geometric idea:

$$
\boxed{
\hat{\bf y}\in\operatorname{Col}({\bf X}),
\qquad
{\bf e}\perp\operatorname{Col}({\bf X})
}
$$
:::
